source_terms: Action: Present an enticing call-to-action with the right context
Apply core principles
Make the product the ad
Be exact and tangible
Present the ask after the context is set
item.claim: For an action objective, whose stated aim is to present an enticing call to action with the right context, Attention is left at the core principles. Branding goes furthest here — "make the product the ad". Connection is to be exact and tangible. Direction carries an ordering instruction rather than a wording one: present the ask after the context has been set.

mechanism.text: The objective's own statement supplies the reason for the ordering: the call to action is to arrive "with the right context", so the context must be established before the ask.

scope.conditions: Campaigns whose marketing objective is action

caveats.text: This is the source's only instruction anywhere about where in an ad the ask should sit, and it is objective-specific. Nothing in the core Direction guidance says the CTA belongs at the end, or anywhere in particular.

"Make the product the ad" is the strongest branding instruction in the table and sits in some tension with the core Connection guidance to build the ad around people's experience. The source does not address the tension.
No evidence is offered for this weighting. It is asserted in a table with no result attached to any cell.

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

source_stated_remedies: Present the ask after the context is set

intra_source_relations.note: 'make the product the ad' pulls against building the ad on people's experience

item.label: objective_weighted_abcds
item.description: The source's second-stage rule: having applied the core ABCDs, vary the emphasis given to each of the four principles according to the campaign's marketing objective — awareness, consideration, action, or all three combined as full funnel.

whole_system_claim.text: Across the four objectives the membership of the framework is constant and only the emphasis moves. Every one of the sixteen cells carries an instruction; where an objective calls for no special treatment of a principle the cell reads "Apply core principles", which happens three times — Direction under awareness, and Attention under both consideration and action. The full-funnel row is the only one with no such cell, and the only one whose instructions include ordering within the ad.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source publishes the matrix and states the two-stage rule ("Great video ads start when you apply the Core ABCDs, but you can optimize your ads for specific marketing objectives"), but it never characterises the matrix's own shape. The claim that membership is constant and only emphasis varies, and the count of where "Apply core principles" falls, are read off the published table by us. They are directly checkable against it, but they are our reading, not the source's statement.

dependencies.nature: each objective variant presupposes the core principles it modifies

source_ref.locator: Google Ads Help, "About the ABCDs of effective video ads", section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", introductory paragraph

tradeoffs.nature: How directly the ad asks. Consideration is to "plant the seed of urgency"; action is to "present the ask after the context is set"; full funnel escalates directness through the ad. This is the source's whole account of how the ask varies with objective.

conflicts.nature: The action row's "Make the product the ad" pulls against the core Connection guideline to build the story on people's experience of the product. The source publishes both and does not address the tension.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The four objectives, the two-stage rule and the sixteen cell contents are the source's. The characterisation of the matrix's shape — constant membership, varying emphasis, three "Apply core principles" cells — is ours, and so are the trade-off and the conflict recorded above. One extraction note matters: the plain-text capture of the Google Ads Help page linearises the table and loses which cell each instruction belongs to, and two rows carry two bullets in a single Connection cell. The cell-to-column mapping used here was resolved by re-fetching the page and reading the table markup, not inferred from reading order.

provenance.section: Section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", introductory paragraph and four-row table

item.label: the_four_question_framework_and_the_three_elements_it_produces
item.description: The source pairs a specification with a procedure. The specification is the three elements a good critique contains: a specific aspect or decision, its relation to an objective or best practice, and how and why it does or does not support that objective. The procedure is four ordered questions — what is the objective; what elements relate to it; are those elements effective; why or why not — which exist to make sure all three elements are produced. The source presents the questions in a fixed downward flow (Figure 2-1, rendered and inspected) and states one permitted variation: the first two may be reversed depending on how the work is being presented.

whole_system_claim.text: The order carries the method. Fixing the objective before looking for elements directs the search, so what counts as pertinent is settled before anyone starts finding fault; running the same four questions in the reverse direction would be an exercise in justifying reactions after the fact. The fourth question is what stops the output being a verdict: it asks for the result the choice will actually produce, and explicitly admits the case where an element serves the objective only in conjunction with others.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source states the four questions, their order, the permitted reversal of the first two, and that they exist to uncover the three elements. It calls the third question "the crux of critical thinking". It does not state that the ordering is what makes the search directed, or contrast the procedure with a reversed one — that argument is ours, inferred from the source's own insistence throughout that objectives are established before analysis begins and from its treatment of after-the-fact justification as preferential critique.

dependencies: the procedure presupposes that an objective exists and is known; where it does not, scs_disc_005 is the source's answer

item.source_warning_ref: sk_disc_0015 — the source warns that the two supplementary questions it offers alongside the four are the main route to scope creep, and that the group must be prepared to end or defer a discussion that leaves scope

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Almost none of this system is ours. The four questions, their order, the reversal rule, the three elements and the claim that the framework is invariant across artifacts are all stated by the source, twice (printed pp. 9 and 33, and again at p. 92 and p. 175). Our contribution is the argument for why the order matters and the grouping of the specification with the procedure as one system rather than two.

provenance.chapter: 1. Understanding Critique; 2. What Critique Looks Like
provenance.section: Critique: The third form of feedback; A Simple Framework for Critique

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
item.question: How does Samara account for the order in which a reader moves through a layout that has no reading structure, and what does that account let a designer do?
item.answer: He accounts for it as a gradient. Compositional flow, or eye path, occurs as the viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast against the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance — contrast restated as resistance — so the eye moves from the area of greatest overall contrast to the least. Because the order is produced by a gradient rather than by position in a structure, a layout with no grid can still have a reading order, and the designer can support the direction by positioning axes or by using graphical forms to point. Practically, he adds that each element to be encountered next must either differentiate from its context to a similar degree, since like things attract attention, or be positioned near where the eye is likely to leave the previous element; and that graphical markers or anchoring points inserted at strategic locations help focus attention and direct the flow.
item.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": compositional flow as decreasing optical resistance; the eye moving from greatest to least contrast; supporting the direction with axes and pointing forms; like things attracting attention; markers and anchoring points.
confounders: assuming reading order in an unstructured layout is arbitrary
treating eye path as a fixed scan pattern independent of the design
assuming the highest-contrast element is simply the largest; his variable is contrast against the field

item.label: the_acuity_derivation_that_generates_both_contrast_levels
item.description: The AA and AAA contrast criteria are two outputs of one stated causal model. A 3:1 baseline is taken from ISO and ANSI standards for standard text and normal vision. Contrast sensitivity loss associated with a level of visual acuity multiplies that baseline: roughly 1.5 at 20/40, giving 4.5:1 for Level AA; the analogous figure at 20/80 gives about 7:1 for Level AAA. The large-text carve-out enters the same model from the other side — larger text with wider strokes is readable at lower contrast, so the requirement is relaxed by one step, which is why the AAA large-text value is exactly the AA general value.

whole_system_claim.text: Every number in the two contrast criteria is one baseline multiplied by a compensation factor, or that baseline relaxed for glyph size. The model is a model of restoring perception for a reader with measurable acuity loss. It contains no term for attention, appeal or communication effectiveness, and the source claims none.

source_ref.section: Understanding SC 1.4.3, Rationale for the Ratios Chosen

dependencies.nature: 4.5:1 is the stated product of the baseline and the 20/40 sensitivity loss
7:1 is the stated product of the same logic at 20/80
the 3:1 carve-out follows from larger, wider-stroked glyphs reading at lower contrast

tradeoffs.nature: the source presents the relaxation as buying authors a wider range of colour choices for large text at the cost of contrast headroom, and separately warns that the trade fails for extraordinarily thin or unfamiliar letterforms

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The derivation itself is the source's own and is stated as a chain in a single passage, so the system type and the whole-system claim are source_explicit. What is ours is the placement of the normative criteria (sk_wcag_0001, sk_wcag_0002) inside it as outputs — the criteria themselves state no derivation, and the passage that does is non-normative. Reading the model as authorising the criteria is therefore a reading, not a citation.

source_terms: Vernacularism
the vernacular

Using vernacular imagery or a vernacular compositional conceit imposes the look of something else onto a communication, embedding it in this new context, either to draw a comparison or, possibly, to comment on the subject being communicated
gestures of this kind often trade on forms associated with low culture, or undesigned visual experiences
item.claim: A further allusive strategy is to appropriate the visual language of common, everyday experience or the stylistic gestures associated with a particular context — the vernacular. Using vernacular imagery or a vernacular compositional conceit imposes the look of something else onto the communication and embeds it in that new context, either to draw a comparison or to comment on the subject being communicated; the source's example is an invitation to an exclusive art auction designed with the brush lettering and graphic devices of supermarket advertising banners. Because vernacular means the ordinary, gestures of this kind often trade on forms associated with low culture or with undesigned visual experience. The source dates the practice to Pop Art, citing Warhol's Brillo boxes and Rosenquist's paintings of spaghetti and household cleaning products.

mechanism.text: The borrowed look carries its origin's associations with it, so placing a subject inside it forces a comparison between the subject and the world the style came from. The gap between the two is the message.

scope.conditions: communications where a comparison with, or comment on, everyday culture is wanted

caveats.text: Vernacularism is defined by cultural reference and does not transfer between cultures. Hatch Show Prints signify the American Midwest, and Victorian illustrated books signify a small independent business, only to audiences who hold those associations.
The source treats the effect as reliable. It offers no case in which the borrowed style is simply read as the thing it was borrowed from.

source_stated_remedies: appropriate a visual language associated with ordinary experience to embed the subject in a new context

positive.description: a poster whose type is aligned to its own edges and then repeated ad hoc on top of itself to evoke the built-up layers of street postings — a poster showing a posting of posters
a fashion show invitation designed to mimic a retail shopping receipt as a comment on high and low commodity culture
a poster celebrating Kansas that appropriates the stylistic language of 1930s Hatch Show Prints

intra_source_relations.note: a named kind of allusive strategy

the great Indian rope trick of numbers
item.claim: Bijapurkar states the structural claim on which most of the book rests: "Consumer demand in the emerging economies is made up of lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot," where developed-market marketers "are used to working with an exactly opposite demand structure — a few people consuming a lot each, adding up to a lot." She draws the consequence explicitly: "neither the pricing paradigms nor the cost structures of their usual, tried and tested global business models are appropriate for India's demand structure." She names the counter-intuitive consequence the "great Indian rope trick of numbers" — a small penetration of a large population produces a large absolute market, so lower-income groups can out-consume higher-income groups in absolute terms.

mechanism.text: Business models encode assumptions about consumption per head. A retail format sized for a catchment that consumes a lot per head will not reach viability in a catchment that consumes little per head, regardless of how many people are in it — which is why, on her account, the first organised retail forays failed and why a small-format chain with an aggregated back end succeeded by "mimicking the structure of the customer demand".

scope.conditions: Stated for India and for emerging markets more generally, on data to 2008. Bijapurkar draws the general form from the BRIC comparison — economies "individually poor but collectively rich" — and cites Goldman Sachs's *Dreaming with the BRICs*.

caveats.text: the two-wheeler evidence was inspected and it holds. Figure 4.1 (rural two-wheeler market) shows penetration falling 42 / 25 / 10 / 2.7 per cent across income groups while household counts rise 7 / 18 / 63 / 66 million, giving two-wheeler numbers of 3.8 / 4.5 / 6.4 / 1.8 million. The lower-middle group therefore does have about 1.6 times the units of the high-income group, exactly as the text claims. Source: Indian Readership Survey 2008

the general claim about business models is argued from a small number of Indian cases (Subhiksha, shampoo sachets, community telephony) with no failure cases and no financial detail. Subhiksha in particular is presented as a success; the chain collapsed shortly after this edition was published, which the book could not know and which is recorded here because the case is load-bearing
SEVERE FRESHNESS RISK. Every figure supporting this object is 2008 or earlier and predates mobile data, e-commerce and digital payments in India

item.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
item.source_locator: Ch. 13 "Semiotics, Symbols, and Vernacular", sections "What does this remind you of?" and "Why is Nigerian spam so sloppy?" (spine 20)
item.question: Godin argues that badly spelled advance-fee scam mail is not incompetent. What is his reading, and what general claim about form does it illustrate?
item.answer: His reading is that the errors are a filter. The mail is sending a signal to people who are skeptical, careful and well-informed: go away. Putting anyone else into the process wastes the sender's time, and they would rather lose you at the beginning than invest in you and lose you at the end. The general claim is that form acts before content does. Busy people scan rather than study, and while scanning they ask what this reminds them of — and the answer decides whether they are the audience and whether the maker is credible, before any argument is considered. So the vernacular of a category — typefaces, photo styles, copy — is a membership signal: you are not people like us if you do not talk the way we expect you to. Note this is an inference about the senders' intent, not a reported finding about their strategy.
item.support: Why is Nigerian spam so sloppy?: because it's not for you; they're sending a signal to people who are skeptical, careful and well-informed: go away; they'd rather lose you at the beginning than invest in you and lose you at the end. What does this remind you of?: we scan instead of study; we want to know if it's for us, and if you're the real deal.
confounders: reading the sloppiness as low effort or poor language skills
treating semiotics as decoration on top of the message rather than as the thing read first

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Narrative Allusions: Vernacularism' (spine 6)
item.question: You are designing an invitation to an exclusive art auction and propose using the brush lettering and graphic devices of supermarket advertising banners. What is the mechanism Samara says makes this work, and what is the limit an extractor should attach to it?
item.answer: That is Samara's own example. The mechanism is that vernacular imagery, or a vernacular compositional conceit, imposes the look of something else onto the communication and embeds it in that new context, either to draw a comparison or to comment on the subject being communicated. Because "vernacular" means the ordinary, such gestures often trade on forms associated with low culture or with undesigned visual experience, and the distance between the borrowed world and the actual subject is what carries the comment. He traces the practice to Pop Art, citing Warhol's Brillo boxes and Rosenquist's paintings of spaghetti and cleaning products. The limit is that the effect is entirely dependent on the audience holding the association: Hatch Show Prints signify the American Midwest, and Victorian illustrated books signify small independent trade, only to people who already read them that way. Samara does not discuss what happens when the borrowed style is simply read as itself.
item.support: "Vernacularism": the auction-invitation example; imposing the look of something else to draw a comparison or comment; the low-culture note; the Pop Art lineage; the Hatch Show Prints and Victorian-illustration examples.
confounders: treating vernacular borrowing as retro styling for its own sake
assuming the association transfers across cultures — every one of his examples is culture-specific
confusing it with pictorialisation; vernacularism borrows a style, it does not depict the subject

source_terms: benefit maximizers
cost-benefit optimizers
cash constrained benefit maximizers
money for value
value for money
item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a segmentation whose axis is not spending power but VALUE ORIENTATION — how a buyer thinks about benefit against cost. Her five: the rich as benefit maximizers, oriented to "money for value", willing to pay more for more, described as "anywhere in the world consumers who just happen to be in India"; the consuming class as cost-benefit optimizers, oriented to "value for money", balancing the two continuously, "very hard to seduce with imagery-oriented brand benefits"; the climbers as cash-constrained benefit maximizers with a fixed price point who shop for the maximum available within it; the aspirants, new and therefore occasional consumers; and the destitute. She claims the model is generic — "this value orientation-based consumer class model is a generic Indian model that works for all businesses" — and demonstrates it across office automation, hospital services, cellphones, education, chemicals and farm equipment.

mechanism.text: Two buyers with the same budget can want opposite things from it: one to spend it all on the most benefit obtainable, another to spend as little of it as will do. Since the offer that wins differs between them while the affordability data does not distinguish them, a segmentation on spending power will place them together and mis-specify the offer for at least one.

scope.conditions: Presented as a generic Indian model applicable across consumer and industrial categories, on NCAER's consumer-classes framework as the underlying population data.

caveats.text: the claim that the model 'works for all businesses' is a strong universal, supported by a series of illustrative applications the author asserts rather than by any validation. No case is given where it failed, and no test is offered

the class labels (rich / consuming class / climbers / aspirants / destitute) come from NCAER; the VALUE-ORIENTATION overlay is the author's. The record keeps the two apart because the first is survey-derived and the second is not

the Nirma case that anchors the climbers segment is a well-known 1980s story told without figures beyond 'outselling it ten to one in tonnage terms', and the harshness of the product ('65 per cent soda ash') is reported as consumer-accepted on the basis of a single quoted rationalisation
population sizes attached to the segments are 2005-06 vintage and predate the period this project operates in
